questions.prompt: Put these steps of creating and deploying a first report project in SSDT, per Lessons 4-5, in the correct order.
items: Install the SSRS extension and create a new Report Server Project in SSDT
Right-click the Reports folder and Add a New Item to create a .rdl report
Open Project Properties and set TargetServerURL to the report server's /reportserver URL
Select Deploy Solution from the Build menu
Confirm the project's folder and report appear in the web portal's Home folder
questions.explain: A Report Server Project needs the SSRS extension installed before the template even appears. Once created, a .rdl report is added via the Reports folder's Add New Item. Before anything can publish, TargetServerURL has to point at the report server's own /reportserver virtual directory, not the web portal. Deploy Solution then publishes everything, and the final check is confirming the folder and report actually landed in the web portal's Home folder.

questions.prompt: A native-mode report server's ReportServerTempDB is deleted by mistake. What happens, and why does it matter?
options: Reporting Services does NOT automatically re-create it on its own — it's specifically called out as handled differently from the ReportServer database — so session data, execution data, and cached reports have nowhere to go until an administrator recreates it
Reporting Services automatically re-creates it the next time anyone browses the web portal
Nothing happens, because ReportServerTempDB only ever stores data that was already scheduled to be deleted anyway
The report server stops running entirely until the whole native-mode installation is reinstalled from scratch
questions.explain: Lesson 2 draws this distinction directly: ReportServerTempDB stores session/execution data, cached reports, and working tables, and background processes periodically clean out old rows — but unlike ReportServer, Reporting Services won't automatically re-create this database if it's missing. Losing it isn't fatal to the whole install, but it does mean temporary data has nowhere to land until someone recreates it manually.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Report Builder is a stand-alone, Office-like application, while SSDT's own report authoring tool inside Visual Studio is called ________.
questions.explain: Report Builder and SSDT's Report Designer build the exact same kind of file — an RDL report definition — but Report Designer is the name of the specific authoring tool that lives inside the Visual Studio-based SSDT environment, organized around Report Server Projects rather than single standalone files.

questions.prompt: Which data region groups data along both rows and columns at once, producing a genuine cross-tabulation rather than a single list of grouped rows?
options: Matrix
Table
List
Chart
Gauge
Indicator
questions.explain: A Table groups data down the page — one grouping dimension, rows only. A Matrix groups both ways, rows and columns, producing the same shape as a pivot table: every combination of row group and column group gets its own cell, with totals in both directions.
questions.distractorExplain: Table is the closest wrong answer because it's also a grouped, tabular data region — but it only has one grouping dimension, down the page. It has no Column groups box the way a Matrix does, so it can never produce a true cross-tab; it can only ever get taller as data grows, never wider the way a Matrix does when a column-group field gains distinct values.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about data sources and datasets, per Lesson 6.
options: A data source is the connection information; a dataset is a query run against that connection
An embedded data source or dataset is saved inside one report only
A shared data source has to be recreated separately inside every report that wants to use it
In Report Builder, you can create a brand-new shared data source from scratch, the same as you can in SSDT
A dataset needs a data source to run against — neither one is useful entirely on its own
questions.explain: A data source is the connection; a dataset is the query that runs against it — always a pair. Embedded means saved inside just that one report. A shared data source is published once and referenced by many reports, which is the opposite of needing to be recreated everywhere — that's exactly the maintenance burden being shared avoids. And in Report Builder, you can only browse to and select an existing shared data source; creating a brand-new one from scratch is something only SSDT's project-based workflow allows.

questions.prompt: Match each Report Builder dialog or pane to what it actually controls, per Lesson 7.
right: Row Groups and Column Groups for whatever data region is currently selected
Data sources, datasets, parameters, and images, all in one tree
Border/fill for the report body, reached by right-clicking the white design-surface area
Page setup and report-level settings, reached by right-clicking the gray area around the design surface
questions.explain: Right-clicking the white body area gets Body Properties (border/fill); right-clicking the gray area around it gets Report Properties (page setup and report-level settings) — mixing these two up is the single most common early mistake. The Grouping pane holds Row Groups/Column Groups for the selected data region, while the Report Data pane holds data sources, datasets, parameters, and images together in one tree.

questions.prompt: A table report looks fine — one page wide — in Design view, but renders across four separate pages when printed. What's the most likely cause?
options: The report body's width, including margins, exceeds the physical page's width — something Design view's canvas size doesn't warn you about, since it has no relationship to the physical page
The dataset query is returning too many rows for a single page
The table is missing a Page Break property on its header row
SSRS caps every printed report at one page unless Report Snapshot is enabled
questions.explain: The design surface's size has no relationship to the physical page — it's elastic and never warns you about print width. A hard page-break renderer paginates against the actual physical page width, so if the report body's width plus margins exceeds that, you get unwanted extra pages. The fix is checking the body's width against the physical page in Report Properties > Page Setup, not the row count or a missing page-break setting.

questions.prompt: A dataset's query reads WHERE StoreID = (@StoreID). An author checks "Allow multiple values" on the StoreID parameter but doesn't touch the query. What happens when a reader selects more than one store?
options: The query breaks, because = can't compare a column against an array of selected values — the WHERE clause has to change to WHERE StoreID IN (@StoreID) to work with a multi-value parameter
The query silently ignores every value except the first one selected
SSRS automatically rewrites = to IN behind the scenes, so nothing breaks
The report runs fine, because = and IN are functionally identical in T-SQL
questions.explain: Once a parameter allows multiple values, its value becomes an array, not a single value. The = operator can't compare a column against an array — the dataset query, any Tablix filters, and any direct display expressions referencing the parameter all have to change (to IN, to the In operator, and to Join(), respectively) to actually work correctly once that checkbox is on.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about cascading parameters, per Lesson 13.
options: A cascading setup is a chain of separate datasets, each filtered by the parameter chosen one level up
The actual filter lives on each dependent dataset's Filters tab, referencing the earlier parameter's value
Parameter order in the Report Data pane's Parameters node is purely cosmetic and doesn't affect runtime behavior
Country must come before State in the Parameters node, since State's dataset filter references [@CountryParameter]
A cascading chain only works if every parameter in it is multi-value
questions.explain: A cascade isn't one property — it's a chain of separate datasets, each one's Filters tab referencing the parameter chosen before it (Expression / Operator / Value, with Value set to [@CountryParameter] or similar). Order is not cosmetic: because State's dataset filter references Country's value, Country genuinely has to come first, or the parameter it references hasn't been chosen yet. And the cascading mechanism itself is identical whether a parameter is single- or multi-value — only the filter's operator (= versus In) changes.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a parameter's Default Values tab offers three options — No default value, Specify values, and ________, which pulls the default from a field in an existing dataset.
questions.explain: Get values from a query points the default at an existing dataset and a field within it, rather than a literal value you type in — useful for defaulting a parameter to something meaningful, like the first row of a lookup dataset or the current fiscal quarter.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order Report Builder actually turns a query variable into a working report parameter, per Lesson 12.
items: Add a WHERE clause like WHERE StoreID = (@StoreID) to the dataset's query
Run the query, and Report Builder prompts for a value to resolve @StoreID
Report Builder automatically creates a matching dataset parameter from that query variable
A report parameter named StoreID appears under the Parameters node in the Report Data pane
questions.explain: Adding the @StoreID placeholder to the query text comes first. Running the query then triggers Report Builder's prompt for a value, since the placeholder is unresolved. From there, Report Builder automatically builds the matching dataset parameter, and finally a report parameter of the same name shows up under Parameters — you never had to build the report parameter by hand.

questions.prompt: What are the four regions that make up the Expression dialog box, per Lesson 17?
options: The expression text area, the Category tree, the Item list, and the Description/Example panel
The expression text area, a live preview pane, a Save button, and a Cancel button
Fields, Parameters, Datasets, and Variables — with no Category tree at all
Category, Item, a syntax-highlighted code editor, and a Run button
The Ribbon, the Report Data pane, the Grouping pane, and the design surface
A search box, an alphabetical function list, a Help button, and the expression text area
questions.explain: The Expression dialog is four regions working together: the expression text area at the top where the actual `=`-prefixed expression gets built; the Category tree on the left (Parameters, Fields, Datasets, Variables, Operators, Common Functions); the Item list in the middle, which changes based on the selected Category; and the Description/Example panel on the right, showing what the selected item does with a real working example.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C lists four of the dialog's actual collections — Fields, Parameters, Datasets, Variables — but those all live inside one region, the Category tree, rather than being four separate regions themselves. The dialog's real four regions are the expression text area, Category, Item, and Description/Example, with Category itself holding Fields/Parameters/Datasets/Variables/Operators/Common Functions as its contents.

questions.prompt: This expression is set on a table row's BackgroundColor property. What does it actually produce when the report runs, and why?
options: Alternating banded rows — MOD 2 returns 1 (true) for odd rows and 0 (false) for even ones, so IIF alternates between the parameter's color and white
Every row the same color, because RowNumber(Nothing) always returns the same value for every row in a table
A runtime error, because IIF can't be used inside a BackgroundColor expression
Every row shaded white, because MOD 2 always evaluates to zero for a table's detail rows
questions.explain: RowNumber(Nothing) counts rows starting at the outermost data region, and MOD 2 returns 1 for odd row numbers, 0 for even ones. Since 0 is treated as False and any nonzero value as True, the IIF alternates between Parameters!RowColor.Value and White — one IIF expression on one property, and every other row comes out shaded. This is exactly the real banding pattern from Lesson 19, with no separate 'conditional formatting' feature involved.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about number, date, and currency formatting in SSRS, per Lesson 21.
options: Every option on the Number page maps to an underlying .NET Framework format string
Typing an invalid format string into Custom causes SSRS to throw a runtime error
You can type any valid .NET format string directly, even for formats the Number page's buttons don't expose
The Format() function is the better choice once a text box needs to mix a formatted value with literal text
Changing a column's Number format also changes the underlying numeric value stored in the dataset
questions.explain: Every Number-page option — Currency, Date, Percentage — is really a .NET format string under the hood, and any valid .NET format string can be typed directly even when the dialog doesn't offer a dedicated button for it. The Format() function is the right tool once a value needs to be mixed with literal text in one expression. An invalid format string doesn't throw an error at all — it falls back to displaying the format string itself as literal text, a useful debugging signal. And formatting is purely a display change; the underlying dataset value never changes.

questions.prompt: Match each Chart Data pane or gauge term to what it actually controls, per Lessons 22-23.
right: What appears along the category (x) axis - each distinct value becomes one data point
Determines how many series the chart draws; empty means exactly one series
The aggregated numeric field(s) actually plotted on the chart
The top-level container that holds one or more gauges (or indicators)
questions.explain: Category Groups controls the category (x) axis, with each distinct value becoming one data point. Series Groups determines how many series get drawn — leave it empty and you get exactly one, fixed at design time. Values holds the aggregated numeric field(s) actually plotted. A Gauge panel is the separate top-level container every gauge (or indicator) always lives inside, independent of the chart vocabulary.

questions.prompt: An author tries to drop a sparkline next to raw, ungrouped detail rows in a table, but SSRS won't allow it there. Why not?
options: A sparkline displays aggregated data, so it has to sit in a cell associated with a group - a group total row, not a per-record detail row
Sparklines can only be added to a Matrix, never to a Table
A sparkline requires at least three series, and a detail row can only ever show one
SSRS treats sparklines as full charts, which can't be nested inside any data region
questions.explain: A sparkline is a chart nested inside a table or matrix cell, and because it displays aggregated data, it has to be associated with a group - a group total row - not a raw, per-record detail row. This trips up newcomers who try to drop one next to ungrouped rows and wonder why it won't take.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an Indicator is essentially a simplified gauge with no frame, scale, or pointer - just icons representing ________.
questions.explain: An indicator strips away the frame, scale, and pointer a gauge has, leaving only states - each one represented by a small icon, optionally with a label - which is exactly what keeps indicators legible at the tiny sizes a table row or matrix cell forces on them.

questions.prompt: An author tries to set a Details row group's ToggleItem to a text box that lives inside that same Details group. What happens, and why?
options: Report Builder won't offer that text box as a valid ToggleItem - the toggle has to sit in the same group as the hidden item, or in an ancestor group above it
It works exactly the same as any other ToggleItem assignment
The report runs, but clicking the toggle deletes the Details group's rows permanently
SSRS automatically moves the text box into the parent group to make the assignment valid
questions.explain: The containing-scope rule says a toggle text box can't be the row or column group it's hiding - it has to sit in the same group as the hidden item, or in an ancestor group above it. To toggle a child group's rows, the toggle text box has to live in a row belonging to the parent group or higher. Get this backwards and Report Builder won't even offer that text box as a valid ToggleItem option.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the difference between a drillthrough report and a subreport, per Lessons 27-28.
options: A drillthrough report's data isn't retrieved until the user actually clicks the link, which usually makes it cheaper to run than a subreport
A subreport's data is retrieved at the same time as the main report's, whether or not anyone looks at it
A drillthrough action's parameter names must match the target report's parameters exactly, including case
A subreport is a separate report that opens in place of the main report, the same way a drillthrough report does
In SSDT's Report Designer, a subreport parameter can always be skipped as long as the subreport has some default value, exactly like in Report Builder
questions.explain: A drillthrough report's data is lazily retrieved only when clicked, making it typically cheaper than a subreport, whose data is retrieved alongside the main report's regardless of whether anyone looks at it. Drillthrough parameter names must match the target report's exactly, including case, or the link fails at run time. A subreport is physically embedded inside the main report's layout, not a separate report that opens in its place - that's the drillthrough behavior, not the subreport's. And the two design tools genuinely differ here: Report Builder tolerates a missing subreport parameter if it has a default, but Report Designer (SSDT) requires every required parameter to be listed.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of wiring up a drillthrough action in the correct order, per Lesson 27.
items: Design and publish the parameterized target (drillthrough) report first
Right-click the source item and open its Properties dialog's Action tab
Select 'Go to report' and browse to the target report
Add a parameter row, mapping the target report's parameter Name to a Value expression from the main report
Run the main report and click the linked item to confirm the target report opens correctly
questions.explain: The target report always gets designed first, since the drillthrough link needs something real to point at. From there, the source item's Action tab is where 'Go to report' and the target report get set, followed by mapping each required parameter's Name to a Value from the main report's own fields. Only after all of that is wired up do you test by running the main report and clicking the link.

questions.prompt: A report's data source prompts for credentials every time it runs, and one of its parameters has no default value set. What happens when you try to create a subscription for it?
options: The New Subscription option isn't even available - a subscription runs unattended, so the data source needs stored (or no) credentials, and every parameter needs a default value
The subscription is created normally, and it prompts for credentials by email each time it fires
The subscription is created, but it silently fails every time it runs without ever showing an error
SSRS automatically assigns a default value of NULL to any parameter missing one
questions.explain: Two requirements have to be met before New Subscription even shows up: the data source must use stored credentials or no credentials, since a subscription runs with nobody there to type in a login, and any parameters must have default values, since nobody's available to fill them in when the subscription fires. Without both, the option simply isn't available at all.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about data-driven subscriptions, per Lesson 31.
options: A data-driven subscription queries a subscriber database at run time to determine recipients, delivery settings, and parameters
The query's result set columns determine what you can map to delivery settings and parameters
The query's result set rows determine how many separate report deliveries get generated
Data-driven subscriptions are available to every user with Browser-level access
Microsoft recommends testing the query directly in SQL Server Management Studio before pasting it into the subscription wizard
questions.explain: A data-driven subscription queries a subscriber database each run to determine recipients, delivery settings, and parameters for that run. Its result set's columns determine what can be mapped to settings, while its rows determine how many deliveries actually get generated - ten thousand rows means ten thousand deliveries. This option is only available to users with advanced permissions, not ordinary Browser-level access. And Microsoft's own advice is to validate the query in SSMS first, since debugging it there is far easier than inside the wizard's query-timeout window.

questions.prompt: Match each scheduling/delivery term to what it actually is, per Lesson 33.
right: Created once and referenced by any number of reports and subscriptions; can be paused and resumed
Defined inline inside one subscription, with no separate item to manage
The service whose job fires when a schedule's trigger time arrives
Polls the event queue and hands a fired schedule's work to the right delivery extension
questions.explain: A shared schedule is created once as its own item and referenced by many reports/subscriptions, and uniquely among the two, it can be paused and resumed. A report-specific schedule is defined inline, with no separate item. Creating either kind writes a SQL Server Agent job that actually fires on time, dropping an event into a queue the Scheduling and Delivery Processor polls (every 10 seconds by default) and hands off to the correct delivery extension.

questions.prompt: An administrator needs to change the service account the report server runs as. Which tool handles that, and why can't the web portal's Site Settings page do it instead?
options: Report Server Configuration Manager - it's the machine-level tool for the service account, URLs, database connection, and the symmetric key; Site Settings only covers day-to-day, browser-based settings like General, Security, and Schedules
Site Settings' General tab - service account changes are just another system-wide default
Either tool works identically, since they both write to the same ReportServer database tables
Neither tool can change it - the service account can only be changed by reinstalling SQL Server Reporting Services
questions.explain: Administration genuinely happens in two separate places. The Report Server Configuration Manager is the machine-level tool: service account, report server and web portal URLs, the database connection, the symmetric key backup, and email delivery setup. The web portal's Site Settings page is the day-to-day, browser-based tool - General, Security, Schedules - and it deliberately can't touch the service account, database connection, or URLs; those stay in Configuration Manager.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about item-level versus system-level security, per Lesson 35.
options: Item-level and system-level role assignments are mutually exclusive - one doesn't grant what the other does
Granting a brand-new user real access to a report server is genuinely a two-part job: an item-level assignment plus a system-level one
Item-level role assignments are inherited down the folder hierarchy from wherever they're set, by default
A system-level role assignment, on its own, makes someone a full system administrator
Breaking inheritance on one report automatically removes security from every other report in the same folder
questions.explain: Item-level (folder hierarchy access) and system-level (server-wide operations, like using Report Builder or shared schedules) role assignments are mutually exclusive, which is exactly why adding a new user is genuinely a two-part job: one assignment for content access, another for site-wide features. Item-level assignments are inherited down the folder hierarchy by default, from Home downward. A system-level assignment is not the same as being a system administrator - it doesn't confer full control on its own. And customizing security (breaking inheritance) on one specific report leaves every other item in that same folder untouched.

questions.prompt: A report runs a genuinely long query and must never touch its data source during business hours, whether or not anyone actually opens the report that day. Which execution mode fits, and why not simple caching instead?
options: Report snapshot - it runs deliberately on a schedule regardless of whether anyone requests the report, while caching only ever runs because a user actually asked for the report first
Cache copies of this report, since a sufficiently long cache-expiration value achieves the exact same thing as a snapshot
Always run with the most recent data, since that's the only mode guaranteed to reflect business hours correctly
Neither mode matters, since the data source can't be protected from queries during business hours regardless of settings
questions.explain: Caching is opportunistic - it happens because a user requested the report, and even the very first request still pays the full query cost. A report snapshot is deliberate: it captures data and layout on a schedule you control, running whether or not anyone's watching, which is exactly the guarantee needed for a report that must not hit its data source during business hours at all.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Reporting Services logs how long each report actually took to process in the report server database's ________ view - one row per execution, with a timing breakdown per processing phase.
questions.explain: ExecutionLog3 is the report server database view holding one row per execution - which report, who ran it, when, which output format, and how many milliseconds each processing phase took. Checking it before and after a change turns 'this feels faster' into an actual number.

questions.prompt: In the capstone suite, OrderDetailByTerritory.rdl's @TerritoryID and @Year parameters are set to Internal instead of a normal visible prompt. Why?
options: The report is only ever opened via the drillthrough action from RegionalSalesSummary.rdl, which already supplies both values - an Internal parameter has no prompt or default because no one is ever meant to type one in
Internal parameters are required any time a parameter's data type is Integer
Internal parameters let the report run faster, since they skip the dataset query entirely
Internal parameters are the only kind SSRS allows on a report built against AdventureWorks2012
questions.explain: OrderDetailByTerritory is never meant to be opened directly with a blank parameter prompt - it only ever receives TerritoryID and Year from the summary report's drillthrough click. Setting both to Internal removes the prompt and default entirely, which is exactly why clicking a matrix cell opens the detail report pre-filtered with no extra prompt at all.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of the capstone report suite to what it actually is, per Lessons 38-39.
left: The matrix data cell's Action property
right: A matrix over AdventureWorksDW2014, driven by a cascading territory-group parameter and a multi-value year parameter
A grouped table over AdventureWorks2012, reachable only via drillthrough
The original OLTP TerritoryID, carried into the warehouse unchanged - the bridge between summary and detail data
Where the drillthrough's 'Go to report' setting and parameter mapping actually live
questions.explain: RegionalSalesSummary.rdl is the matrix over the warehouse database, driven by TerritoryGroup and CalendarYear. OrderDetailByTerritory.rdl is the grouped table over the OLTP database, reachable only through drillthrough. SalesTerritoryAlternateKey is DimSalesTerritory's preserved copy of the original TerritoryID - the bridge column that makes the drillthrough possible. And the matrix data cell's Action property is specifically where 'Go to report' and the TerritoryID/Year parameter mapping are configured.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building the capstone report suite in the correct order, per Lesson 39.
items: Build RegionalSalesSummary.rdl with its three datasets, the TerritoryGroup and CalendarYear parameters, and the matrix layout
Build OrderDetailByTerritory.rdl with its dataset and its two Internal parameters, TerritoryID and Year
Select the matrix's data cell and set its Action to Go to report, mapping TerritoryID and Year from the summary report's fields
Preview RegionalSalesSummary.rdl and confirm the matrix renders real numbers for a chosen territory group and year
Click a data cell and confirm the drillthrough opens OrderDetailByTerritory.rdl already filtered, with no parameter prompt
Deploy both reports to the same folder on the Report Server so the drillthrough resolves after publishing
questions.explain: The summary report is built first, since the drillthrough needs a source. The detail report comes next, with its parameters set to Internal because they're only ever supplied by the summary report. Only once both reports exist does the matrix cell's Action get wired up to pass TerritoryID and Year. Previewing the summary report first confirms its own data and parameters work, then clicking a cell confirms the drillthrough itself. Deployment to the same folder comes last, since the drillthrough only resolves correctly once both reports are actually published together.
